source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Chapter XI, “Making Their Beds Before They Could Lie On Them”
A lesson Washington says he learned from General Samuel C. Armstrong, president of Hampton Institute

source.excerpt: It is now long ago that I learned this lesson from General Armstrong, and resolved that I would permit no man, no matter what his colour might be, to narrow and degrade my soul by making me hate him. With God’s help, I believe that I have completely rid myself of any ill feeling toward the Southern white man for any wrong that he may have inflicted upon my race.
trail: Downloaded the complete Project Gutenberg text of Up from Slavery ↗ and searched it. The sentence appears once, in chapter XI, exactly as quoted above.
Wikiquote’s Booker T. Washington page ↗ lists the same line in its sourced Up From Slavery (1901) section and gives the same chapter and chapter title, independently of the Gutenberg text.
Wikiquote additionally records that the line was quoted in a shortened form as early as 1904, and lists three further paraphrases in circulation — see the fact-check below.
Confirmed Washington’s dates (1856–1915) and his Tuskegee tenure from the same Wikiquote page and from Wikipedia ↗.
source.excerptNote: The quotation as it circulates begins mid-sentence. Washington’s own sentence opens by naming where the resolution came from — General Armstrong, the president of Hampton Institute, under whom Washington had studied.

author.name: Booker T. Washington
author.heading: About Booker T. Washington
author.metaLine: 1856–1915 · American educator, author and first leader of Tuskegee
author.bio: Booker Taliaferro Washington was born into slavery in Virginia and freed as a child. He worked in salt furnaces and coal mines, walked much of the way to Hampton Institute to get an education, and in 1881 was named the first leader of the new Tuskegee Institute, which he led until his death. Up from Slavery (1901) made him internationally famous; his strategy of accommodation with the white South made him, in the same years, one of the most contested figures in American public life.

misattribution.heading: The versions that are not his
misattribution.intro: Washington is the right author and the sentence is genuinely his. What travels is often a rewrite. Wikiquote ↗ records these forms alongside the original.

items.who: “I permit no man to narrow and degrade my soul by making me hate him”
items.why: Per Wikiquote, this trimmed version was already being quoted in Charm and Courtesy in Conversation (1904) by Frances Bennett Callaway. It drops the clause that carries the point — “no matter what his colour might be”.

items.who: “I shall allow no man to belittle my soul by making me hate him”
items.why: Listed by Wikiquote ↗ among the paraphrases. “Belittle” is not Washington’s word; he wrote “narrow and degrade”.

items.who: “I let no man drag me down so low as to make me hate him”
items.why: Another of the paraphrases Wikiquote lists. This one is a different sentence entirely.

misattribution.truthLine: The authentic wording is the one on this page, from chapter XI of Up from Slavery (1901) ↗ — and it begins, in Washington’s own sentence, with the man he learned it from.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Washington was born into slavery in Virginia and freed as a child — his own book puts his birth year no closer than “1858 or 1859”. By the time he wrote this he had led Tuskegee for twenty years and was the most powerful Black public figure in America — and the most criticised, by those who thought his accommodation with the white South conceded too much.

The sentence sits inside that argument. Read one way it is a refusal to be deformed by other people’s cruelty; read another it is the doctrine his opponents attacked. Washington puts it as a practical resolution rather than a moral pose: hatred is something that narrows and degrades you.
detailsBody: The chapter is not about the school’s building years; it is about visits from the people who had made the school possible. General J.F.B. Marshall, Hampton’s treasurer, who had lent Tuskegee the first two hundred and fifty dollars; Miss Mary F. Mackie, who had given Washington the “sweeping” examination when he arrived at Hampton; and finally General Armstrong himself.

What Washington takes from that visit is a surprise. He had assumed a man who had fought the Southern white man must cherish some bitterness toward the white South; instead he found him “as anxious about the prosperity and the happiness of the white race as the black”, and never once heard him speak a bitter word against him. “From his example in this respect,” Washington writes, “I learned the lesson that great men cultivate love, and that only little men cherish a spirit of hatred.” The sentence people quote is the next one but one — and readers have taken its claim, that he had rid himself entirely of ill feeling toward the Southern white man, at face value or not for more than a century.
context.pull: It is now long ago that I learned this lesson from General Armstrong.
